book.title: The AI Ready School
book.author: Stephen R. Jordan
book.volume: Volume X of The Operating Discipline for AI Library

name: Counseling, College, and Career
blurb: Every spring, many high school graduates are admitted to college, plan to go, and never show up in the fall. Researchers call this summer melt.
title: Counseling, College, and Career
answer: Every spring, many high school graduates are admitted to college, plan to go, and never show up in the fall. Researchers call this summer melt.

papers.why: High school example of AI for career prep with dependency risk.
papers.title: Generative AI in high school English career preparation units: Student interactions, perceptions, and ethical concerns
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: High school ELA units used AI for resumes and text-based mock interviews. Positive perceptions; many students questioned and revised AI output, others became passive or dependent; concerns about generic responses.

papers.why: Relevant to CTE and career pathway ideas.
papers.title: Needs and requirements for an additional AI qualification during dual vocational training: Results from studies of apprentices and teachers
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Mixed methods: 12 vocational teachers and 746 apprentices in Germany want an AI qualification covering basic AI concepts, taught blended and action-oriented.

papers.why: Supports the book's argument that AI readiness includes human capabilities.
papers.title: Rethinking the entwinement between artificial intelligence and human learning: What capabilities do learners need for a world with AI?
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Eleven-author dialogue on what capabilities learners need in a world with AI: cognitive, humanistic, and social, not only AI literacy.

papers.why: Supports teacher and student co-design in pilots.
papers.title: How can we design for learning in an AI world?
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Argues educators and learners should co-design learning for an AI world using a capability approach.

papers.title: Are Artificially Intelligent Conversational Chatbots Uniformly Effective in Reducing Summer Melt? Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, 4,442 admitted students: chatbot outreach helped most with financial aid steps, concentrated among first-generation students.

papers.title: Nudging at scale: Experimental evidence from FAFSA completion campaigns
papers.venue: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: Two RCTs reaching 800,000 students: national and state nudge campaigns had no effect on aid or enrollment.

papers.title: A National-Level Informational Experiment to Promote Enrollment in Selective Colleges
papers.venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, 785,000 students: brochures, emails, texts, and fee waivers did not change enrollment.

papers.title: Digital Messaging to Improve College Enrollment and Success
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: Cluster RCTs: national texting was mostly null; school-based texting from students' own counselors in Texas raised college steps and enrollment for some groups.

papers.title: Customized Nudging to Improve FAFSA Completion and Income Verification
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: Multidistrict experiment: personalized texts using FAFSA status data improved completion and college matriculation.

papers.title: Parental Influences on Postsecondary Decision Making: Evidence From a Text Messaging Experiment
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT: text outreach raised on-time enrollment 3.1 points; adding parents did not add effect.

papers.title: How an Artificially Intelligent Virtual Assistant Helps Students Navigate the Road to College
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: Field experiment: an AI text chatbot helped admitted students finish pre-enrollment tasks; on-time enrollment up 3.3 percentage points with less staff time.

papers.title: Summer nudging: Can personalized text messages and peer mentor outreach increase college going among low-income high school graduates?
papers.venue: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT: automated personalized texts and peer mentor outreach in the summer after graduation raised college enrollment for students with less counseling access.

children.name: Reminders That Work, and Reminders That Do Not
children.blurb: Reminders about college and financial aid steps work best when they come from someone the student knows, such as their own counselor, rather than from a large outside campaign.

children.name: Where the Counselor's Time Goes
children.blurb: Counselors lose much of their day to scheduling, paperwork, testing coordination and routine questions, work that does not need their expertise.

children.name: Scholarships and Scams
children.blurb: Scholarship searches can help students pay for college, and AI can help them organize applications and deadlines, but scholarship scams are a real risk.

children.name: Financial Aid in Plain Language
children.blurb: Financial aid in plain language means using AI to draft clear, simple guides to the FAFSA and to explain common problems families face, while keeping official details sourced from Federal Student Aid and having a person help with the form itself.

children.name: Keeping Seniors on Track Over the Summer
children.blurb: Summer melt is the loss of college-bound students between graduation and enrollment, and it falls hardest on those with the least support at home.

children.name: Course Plans and Graduation Audits
children.blurb: Course plans and graduation audits use AI tools to help students choose courses that keep college, career, and trade options open, and to catch missing credits before graduation.

children.name: Exploring Colleges, Careers, Trades, and the Military
children.blurb: Exploring colleges, careers, trades, and the military means helping every student see the full range of paths after school, not only four year college.

children.name: Essays, Resumes, and Interviews
children.blurb: AI can help students brainstorm college essays, organize ideas, and practice resumes and interviews, but it must never write the essay or replace the student's own voice.

children.name: Recommendation Letters
children.blurb: AI can help counselors and teachers draft the structure of recommendation letters or suggest ways to describe a student's strengths, but the writer must supply the specific stories and details that make a letter meaningful.

children.name: Supporting First Generation Families
children.blurb: Supporting first generation families means giving students whose parents did not attend college extra help with applications, financial aid, and campus life, because their families may not know how these systems work.

children.name: Postsecondary Planning for Students With Disabilities
children.blurb: Students with disabilities need postsecondary planning that prepares them for a different accommodations landscape, where colleges and employers expect students to request support on their own.

children.name: Guarding Against Steering
children.blurb: Guarding against steering means watching whether college and career guidance tools push students toward some paths and away from others based on old patterns in their data.

children.name: Tracking Outcomes
children.blurb: Tracking outcomes means a school follows what happens to its graduates after they leave, using a service that reports college enrollment and whether students persisted.

sections.body: This section is about the work of school counselors as students move from high school to college, careers, trades, or the military, and about what AI is actually doing in that work. The book describes AI sending reminders, answering student questions, and helping with steps like financial aid and enrollment, as in the trial where a chatbot reminded admitted students and on time enrollment rose by 3.3 percentage points with less staff time. It also covers course planning, graduation audits, essays, resumes, interviews, recommendation letters, and support for first generation families. The section treats counselors as carrying some of the heaviest caseloads in education, often far above the 250 students per counselor recommended by the American School Counselor Association, so students with the least help at home often get the least help at school.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that personal messages from a student's own school, tied to the student's real situation, have improved college steps and enrollment, while national campaigns that sent generic messages to hundreds of thousands of students had no effect. The difference it names is the connection to a real counselor and real deadlines, and it warns that without a personal connection and real data, reminders become noise. The rule it holds to is that AI can extend counselors' reach only if it is used to reach the students who need it most, and that counselors approve every course plan and graduation audit. The common failure pattern is the generic campaign, where a district counts messages sent as success and sees no change in outcomes, and the book says the number of students with accounts on a planning platform is not enough.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from what works and what does not in reminders, through where the counselor's time goes, into the practical tasks of scholarships and scams, financial aid in plain language, and keeping seniors on track over the summer. They then cover course plans and graduation audits, exploring colleges, careers, trades, and the military, essays, resumes, and interviews, recommendation letters, and supporting first generation families, with postsecondary planning for students with disabilities and guarding against steering addressing students who need extra care. Tracking outcomes closes the set by asking for enrollment and persistence data by student group, along with FAFSA completion and summer outreach records, so a board can see who actually gets help. A teacher would go to the essay, resume, and interview pages, a counselor to the reminder, financial aid, and summer pages, a leader to the outcomes and steering pages, and a parent to the first generation and financial aid pages.
